historyReviewBoundary: All 115 histories have author source checks. Final independent review covered metadata and numerical checks for all 115 classes, 12 deeper class targets and source-gap samples in seven classes. It did not independently verify every passage of every cited source.

history.name: Second-generation antipsychotics

starting.description: In a tricyclic antidepressant-screening program researchers unexpectedly encountered neuroleptic activity; clozapine was subsequently identified. Its clinical antipsychotic effects without the expected extrapyramidal profile became a benchmark for later drugs. Separately, Janssen recalls pursuing an improved pipamperone, and Otsuka reports that clinical observations with OPC-4392 prompted its aripiprazole branch.

inspiration.description: Unexpected neuroleptic effects among screened synthetic tricyclics, clozapine's observed clinical and receptor-binding profiles, effects of pipamperone and ritanserin, existing neuroleptic chemical leads, and OPC-4392 clinical results and dopamine-autoreceptor biology informed distinct lines of development.

steps.description: During a tricyclic antidepressant screen, researchers unexpectedly observed neuroleptic properties and subsequently identified clozapine.

Clozapine's atypical preclinical and clinical profile challenged an assumed requirement for extrapyramidal effects and became a model for later antipsychotics. A review describes industry attempts to emulate its observed receptor profile and names olanzapine, quetiapine and risperidone as resulting agents.

A later controlled comparison in treatment-resistant patients reported greater response to clozapine than to chlorpromazine plus benztropine, contributing clinical evidence for the benchmark described by Hippius.

In a distinct line, Janssen recalls seeking a more potent version of clinically tested pipamperone and combining the properties of ritanserin and haloperidol. A company researcher's presentation describes a medicinal chemistry program based initially on other established neuroleptics, yielding the serotonin/dopamine antagonist risperidone.
In another branch, Otsuka pursued presynaptic autoreceptor agonism, developed and clinically tested OPC-4392, and used its observed benefits and limitations to inform a subsequent program.

The company deliberately screened for both presynaptic and postsynaptic activities, resulting in aripiprazole; subsequent mechanistic analysis characterized it as a D2 partial agonist. The numbered steps group branches rather than assert that each branch began after the preceding one.

design.description: Researchers sought compounds emulating aspects of clozapine's receptor profile, although Janssen personally denied clozapine influenced him. Janssen built a distinct benzisoxazole series around established neuroleptic leads and selected combined serotonin/dopamine antagonism; he described seeking an improved pipamperone and a combination of ritanserin- and haloperidol-like properties. For aripiprazole, Otsuka sought a different activity profile, combining earlier autoreceptor agonism with stronger postsynaptic antagonism, and screened new compounds accordingly.

circumstances.description: The neuroleptic activity encountered during the antidepressant screen was unexpected; the subsequent aripiprazole search for a combined activity profile was planned after clinical observations with OPC-4392.

limits: S1 directly describes the aripiprazole branch and does not establish a common synthetic scaffold or identical discovery path for the other class members.
S4 describes a distinct risperidone chemical program based on earlier neuroleptics, not a claim that risperidone is a clozapine structural derivative.

S5 connects olanzapine and quetiapine to the wider clozapine-profile strategy at the class level, but does not reconstruct each company's detailed chemical or assay sequence; structural or pharmacological similarity alone does not prove a particular synthetic route.
conflicts: Hippius's abstract dates clozapine's discovery to 1958; his narrative describes a 1958 screening program followed by identification in 1959. The precise chemical discovery date is not resolved here.

Janssen recalls clozapine being shelved until after Sandoz acquired Wander; Hippius dates that acquisition to 1972 and cites clinical/pharmacological reports from 1969–1971. The retrospective chronology is unresolved, and those original reports were not read.

S5's broad retrospective connects risperidone with agents modeled on clozapine's receptor profile, while Janssen says clozapine never influenced him personally and instead highlights pipamperone and ritanserin/haloperidol. The different perspectives and scope are unresolved; his personal statement does not establish what every company researcher knew.
Janssen called risperidone a typical rather than atypical neuroleptic. This conflicts with the frozen conventional second-generation grouping but does not change the assigned cohort.
gaps: Company-level original discovery records for olanzapine and quetiapine were not read; S5 describes the general clozapine-profile strategy, not each program's full causal sequence.
The primary OPC-4392 clinical trials and original autoreceptor reports have not been independently read.
Hippius's 1969–1971 primary clozapine clinical and pharmacological reports were not read; his 1999 paper is a retrospective. The 1988 comparative trial was read separately.

The original Janssen 1988 pharmacology report and the full 2003 risperidone discovery retrospective were not read; the latter was available only as an abstract. The exact priority and causal role of individual LSD and receptor assays remain unresolved.

humanContributionInterpretation.summary: OPC-4392 clinical effects and limitations prompted a revised therapeutic hypothesis leading to aripiprazole.
humanContributionInterpretation.scope: A defined branch within a heterogeneous class; substantial rational and laboratory development followed.
